comparison: Perfect agreement on neuronal isolation and culture methodology (C14-C16, C91-C98). Both evaluations affirm successful isolation from aged animals and accept the dendritic arborization findings. Peer reviewers explicitly praised this as 'quite rare and commendable.'

Strong agreement on age-related hyperexcitability findings (C17-C23, C68-C69, C99). Both evaluations support the RMP depolarization, increased spontaneous firing, and unchanged input resistance. Peer reviewers described evidence as 'convincing' and data as 'lovely, crisp.'

Complete agreement on increased action potential firing and reduced rheobase (C24-C27, C70, C100-C103). Both evaluations affirm the stimulus-response data and loss of spike adaptation. Peer reviewers praised 'the rigor of the current-clamp and voltage-clamp experiments.'

Full agreement on neuronal subtype classification and distribution shifts (C28-C40, C71, C104-C110). Both evaluations accept the methodology and finding that electrical changes occur within each subtype. Peer reviewers found the subtype analysis 'interesting, and informative.'

Agreement on reduced M current density findings (C45-C47, C72), though peer review also includes KCNQ2 protein data (C3, C48-C49) and broader KCNQ mechanism claims. Both evaluations accept the voltage-clamp measurements and link to decreased KCNQ2/3 activity.

Partial overlap on KCNQ2 protein findings (C48-C49). OpenEval focuses on the paradoxical protein increase and speculative mechanisms (C84-C85), while peer review groups this with M current data. Both accept the Western blot findings without challenge.

Perfect agreement on correlation analyses (C50-C57). Both evaluations accept the statistical approach showing M current correlates with electrical properties in young/middle-aged neurons but not in old neurons. Peer reviewers did not question these findings.

Strong agreement on specificity of KCNQ changes (C58-C61). Both evaluations accept that other K+ and Na+ currents remain unchanged with age. Peer reviewers implicitly accepted this specificity as part of the overall KCNQ-focused conclusion.

Agreement on linopirdine experiments (C62-C63, C87). Both evaluations support that KCNQ blockade mimics aging effects. OpenEval notes limitations (C86), while peer review focuses on the positive evidence supporting decreased KCNQ2/3 activity as a 'major contributor.'

Strong agreement on retigabine rescue experiments (C64-C66, C73, C119). Both evaluations affirm that KCNQ activation reverses age-related hyperexcitability. Peer reviewers explicitly stated this as a major conclusion with 'solid evidence.'

Agreement on overall significance and main conclusions (C1-C2, C67, C89-C90, C123). Both evaluations affirm this as an important study demonstrating age-related peripheral sympathetic neuron changes. Peer reviewers described it as 'compelling and detailed evidence' with broad implications.

Partial overlap on background literature (C4-C13). OpenEval focuses on established sympathetic aging literature, while peer review emphasizes the conceptual advance of studying peripheral neurons. Both accept the contextual framing as appropriate.

Strong agreement on comparative literature context (C74-C82, C120-C122). Both evaluations accept the cross-species and cross-system contextualization of KCNQ involvement in aging. Peer reviewers did not challenge the literature synthesis.

Disagreement on mechanistic speculation (C41, C83-C85). OpenEval labels these as uncertain/speculative hypotheses. Peer reviewers explicitly criticized lack of mechanistic insights, stating 'the effect is more of an epi-phenomenon of unclear insight,' directly challenging the mechanistic claims.

Agreement on limitations and future directions (C88). Both evaluations accept acknowledged limitations (C86) and suggestions for future work. OpenEval notes these represent speculation/future work rather than current findings.

Minimal overlap on KCNQ background (C42-C44, C113). OpenEval groups this with M current measurements, while peer review treats KCNQ regulation literature as accepted foundational knowledge. Both accept this background without challenge.

Minimal overlap on compensatory mechanisms (C84-C85). OpenEval notes these as speculative, while peer review groups with mechanistic uncertainty. Both recognize these as speculative rather than established findings.

Minimal overlap on KCNQ specificity claim (C83). OpenEval emphasizes this strengthens the KCNQ-specific conclusion, while peer review includes it with mechanistic speculation that was criticized as insufficient.

Minimal overlap on linopirdine limitations (C86). OpenEval acknowledges this as a limitation of the pharmacological approach, while peer review groups it with acknowledged limitations that were accepted.
Minimal overlap on retigabine mechanism (C116-C118). OpenEval includes this as supporting the pharmacological validation, while peer review treats it as accepted background on KCNQ pharmacology.

Minimal overlap on causal role conclusion (C66, C73). OpenEval emphasizes the gain-of-function experiment supports causality, while peer review groups this with the broader pharmacological validation evidence.
Minimal overlap on main conclusion C3. OpenEval groups this with overall conclusions, while peer review includes it with KCNQ mechanism findings. Both support the claim.
Minimal overlap on main conclusion C2. OpenEval groups this with overall significance, while peer review includes it with hyperexcitability findings. Both strongly support the claim.

Minimal overlap on comparative context C76. OpenEval includes this in broad literature review, while peer review focuses on the conceptual advance of studying peripheral neurons. Both accept the contextualization.
